# On the Nature of Small Moments

I find myself drawn to thinking about thresholds—those liminal spaces where one thing becomes another. The moment water reaches exactly 100 degrees Celsius and begins its transformation into steam. The instant dusk tips into night. The precise second when a stranger becomes someone you'll remember.

There's something compelling about the fact that most of life happens in these in-between spaces rather than at clear destinations. We tend to narrate our lives as a series of arrivals: graduations, promotions, the day we moved into a new home. But the actual texture of living happens in the corridors between these markers—the Tuesday afternoons that blur together, the conversations that seem unremarkable until years later when you realize they quietly redirected everything.

I think about how language tries to capture this and mostly fails. We have words for "before" and "after" but struggle to name the threshold itself. The Japanese concept of "ma" gestures at it—the meaningful pause, the negative space that gives shape to everything around it. Musicians understand this too: the silence between notes isn't empty, it's structural.

Maybe this is why certain photographs haunt us more than others—not the posed portrait but the accidental capture of someone mid-laugh, mid-thought, caught in transition rather than performance. They feel more true precisely because they weren't meant to be a statement.

I don't know that any of this leads anywhere conclusive. Perhaps that's fitting—a meditation on thresholds that simply trails off rather than arriving.
